A.explanation: No heat supply describes an adiabatic change, but $p\Delta V$ work can still occur when thermal energy is supplied.

B.explanation: The rate of expansion does not appear in $W = p\Delta V$; the same $p$ and $\Delta V$ give the same work whether fast or slow.

C.explanation: If $p$ stays constant, a single pressure value can multiply $\Delta V$ to give the work done by the gas.

D.explanation: At constant temperature an expanding gas decreases in pressure, so a single $p$ cannot be used in $p\Delta V$.

hints: Notice the expression $p\Delta V$ uses one single value of pressure $p$ multiplied by the volume change $\Delta V$.
Recall that gas work comes from $force \times distance$, which for a piston becomes $pA \times \Delta x$, so $p$ must be factorised out.
Ask what would happen to $p$ if temperature were constant while $V$ increases, and what that implies for using one value of $p$.
walkthrough: Start with mechanical work: $W = F\Delta x$ for a force pushing through a distance.
For a gas in a cylinder with piston area $A$, $F = pA$ and the piston moves $\Delta x$, so $W = pA\Delta x$.
Since $A\Delta x = \Delta V$, this becomes $W = p\Delta V$ only if the same $p$ acts throughout the whole $\Delta x$.
If $p$ changes during expansion, work is the area under the $p$-$V$ graph, not a simple $p$ times $\Delta V$ rectangle.
Constant temperature expansion makes $p$ fall as $V$ rises, and rate of expansion or heat supply do not by themselves keep $p$ fixed.
Hence $p$ must remain constant for the simple product to apply. This is option C.
